Our proof focuses on establishing the existence of a point of infinite order on a given genus 2 curve, and we achieve this by demonstrating the presence of an elliptic curve within the curve's algebraic family, coupled with an infinite number of points defined over rational numbers. Ultimately, our proof culminates in the discovery of an elliptic curve of rank 1 within the curve's algebraic family, thereby establishing the existence of a point of infinite order on the original genus 2 curve. This approach is particularly relevant for estimating the effects of initial conditions on long-run outcomes. A key aspect of this framework is the relationship between the set of moment conditions and the parameters of interest, which we term the 'validity-parameter identification nexus.' This nexus is used to classify the sources of weak identification, including situations where the moment conditions are either overly broad or too narrowly focused. A simulation study highlights the implications of weak identification for panel data models, demonstrating that even small samples can exhibit biased estimates and large standard errors. Ultimately, our research emphasizes the importance of carefully selecting moment conditions to avoid the pitfalls of weak identification. We establish that for any given function $f$ that maps natural numbers to real numbers, there exists a large enough number $n$ such that the sum of the first $n$ terms of the sequence defined by $a_k = f(k) - f\left(\frac{k}{2} \right) - f\left(\frac{k}{3}\right) - f\left(\frac{k}{5}\right)$ is less than 1 for all $k$ in $\bar{S}$.  This result generalizes a previous finding by Erdős and Surányi.  In particular, it shows that the number $2^{o(n)}$ in their work can be replaced with $n^\epsilon$ for any given positive number $\epsilon$, no matter how small.  The proof relies on the concept of random walks on groups and the application of Lov\'asz Local Lemma.  Additionally, it yields a more general statement concerning random walks on groups, which may be of independent interest.  This research was conducted in collaboration with Terence Tao.  His contributions to the problem's formulation and solution are acknowledged.  The paper also includes a note on the connection between the problem and the concept of Sidon sets.  Furthermore, it provides an example of a function $f$ for which the sum of the first $n$ terms of the associated sequence is greater than 2 for an extremely large value of $n$.  This example is derived from the properties of prime numbers and the concept of relative prime numbers. looks familiar or not, it's a well-established fact that people tend to perceive patterns in random data, a phenomenon known as pattern perception.  This study investigates how people's tendency to see patterns in noise influences their ability to recognize faces, specifically examining whether perceiving patterns in faces enhances or detracts from facial recognition accuracy.  To this end, we created a set of images with varying levels of pattern perception, ranging from none to extreme, and used a large dataset of faces to test facial recognition systems.  Our findings show that faces with moderate levels of pattern perception are more easily recognized than those without, while faces with high levels of pattern perception are more difficult to recognize.  We also discovered that faces with patterns are more resistant to adversarial attacks than those without, suggesting that incorporating pattern noise into facial datasets could improve the robustness of facial recognition systems.  Overall, our research highlights the significance of considering the inherent patterns found in faces when developing facial recognition technology.  Code and data are available at https://github.com/kuangruipeng/face-pattern. The course focused on the application of quantum group techniques to the study of classical integrable systems, specifically the KdV hierarchy. I present an introduction to the fundamentals of the subject, starting with the classical definition of the quantum group $U_q\bigl(\mathfrak{g}\bigr)$ associated with a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ and its representation theory. I then discuss the relationship between the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and the KdV hierarchy, exploring how the quantum algebra's generators act as symmetries of the system. I also examine the connection between the quantum group and the classical S-matrix theory, using the example of the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ to derive the S-matrix of the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ KdV hierarchy. I conclude by discussing the connection between the quantum group and the algebraic structure of the hierarchy's soliton solutions. I also provide an appendix detailing the derivation of the S-matrix of the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ KdV hierarchy. I hope this material will be a useful resource for students and researchers interested in the intersection of quantum groups and integrable systems.   We investigated this time for two particles connected by a general 
  bosonic channel, determining that it is directly proportional to 
  the channel's output noise and the average photon number in the

  For a lossy channel, this time is equivalent to the channel's 
  transmission time, while for a thermal channel, it is greater than 
  the channel's transmission time. 
  We also found that the entanglement distillation time is 
  conserved under unitary transformations of the channel and 
  environments. 
  Furthermore, we established that the minimum entanglement distillation 
  time for a bosonic channel is determined by its symmetrized 
  output Wigner function, specifically through the positive 
  semi-definite matrix constructed from the symmetrized Wigner function 
  and the identity matrix. 
  This result provides a practical method for calculating the minimum 
  entanglement distillation time for various channels, including 
  lossy, thermal, and amplified channels. 
  For a thermal channel, we found that the entanglement distillation 
  time is directly proportional to the channel's temperature and 
  the average photon number in the environments. 
  We also derived an inequality relating the entanglement distillation 
  time to the channel's output noise and the number of modes in the 
  environments. 
  This inequality is analogous to the Holevo bound, 
  which relates the classical capacity of a channel to the von Neumann 
  entropy of the channel's output and the entropy of the environments. 
  This research expands on previous findings by Janse van Rensburg and 
  Schumacher, who investigated the minimum entanglement distillation 
  time for a lossy channel.

  training autonomous agents in complex environments, but it faces significant
  challenges in distributed settings.  A major obstacle in MARL is the issue of
  credit assignment, which arises when an agent's actions have far-reaching
  consequences, making it difficult to pinpoint the causal link between past
  actions and current rewards.  This problem is compounded in multi-agent
  settings, where the interactions between agents can lead to complex causal
  relationships.  To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called
  Causal Policy Gradient (CPG), which utilizes causal graphs to guide policy
  gradient updates and selectively ignores irrelevant information.  By leveraging
  causal relationships, CPG provides a more accurate estimation of expected
  policy gradients and significantly improves the performance of MARL.  Our

We further demonstrate the practical efficacy of CPG through extensive experiments, which show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin.   where two self-interested players must choose between cooperation and defection. 
  In this study, we examine the Prisoner's Dilemma game in a dynamic environment 
  with shifting population sizes, where players can either cooperate or defect in 
  a single-shot encounter. 
  We investigate the evolution of cooperation using evolutionary game theory, 
  where players' strategies are determined by random mutations and encounters

  majority of encounters result in losses for the cooperative player. 
  Specifically, cooperation is stable when the population grows by at least 1.5 
  times per generation, and the cost of cooperation is less than the benefit 
  multiplied by the expected number of future encounters.

  demonstrating that cooperation can emerge and persist in dynamic populations. 
  This finding challenges the conventional view that cooperation is unlikely to 
  evolve in Prisoner's Dilemma games. 
  Our study's implications for the evolution of cooperation in real-world 
  populations are discussed.

Utilizing the galactic center as a case study, we investigate how discrete symmetries impact the interpretation of annihilation signals.  Discrete symmetries can significantly affect the dark matter annihilation interpretation by leading to multiple, nearly indistinguishable scenarios that could be misinterpreted as variations in annihilation cross-section, dark matter mass, or astrophysical density profiles.  This ambiguity can be mitigated by considering multiple annihilation channels, as different channels yield distinct spectral patterns.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the application of discrete symmetries to the galactic center can be extended to other environments, such as dwarf galaxies, and that future gamma-ray experiments will be able to distinguish between certain scenarios.  Ultimately, our findings underscore the importance of accounting for discrete symmetries in dark matter annihilation analyses, and the potential benefits of combining gamma-ray data with other astrophysical and theoretical constraints.  By doing so, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of dark matter and its properties.  We provide a Python code, DiscreteSymmetry, for calculating dark matter annihilation spectra under discrete symmetries, available on GitHub.  This code can be used to analyze dark matter annihilation signals in various environments, including the galactic center, dwarf galaxies, and galaxy clusters. This could be achieved by training the algorithms on simulated spectra, and then applying them to real gamma-ray data.  This approach could provide valuable insights into the properties of dark matter, and potentially reveal its presence through gamma-ray signals.   yet the privacy cost incurred when performing DP analysis often needs 
  careful consideration. The interplay between the privacy budget, data 
  characteristics, and learning algorithm significantly affects the outcome. 
  This paper delves into the relationship between the privacy budget and the 
  accuracy of machine learning models, specifically focusing on how the 
  DP framework's sensitivity metric influences the outcome. We demonstrate 
  that the expected risk of DP models can be bounded by the sum of two 
  terms: the first is independent of the data, while the second is 
  directly related to the data's noise and the algorithm's sensitivity. 
  We further establish that this bound is not merely an asymptotic 
  result, but rather a tight guarantee that can be achieved through a 
  DP algorithm that is statistically and computationally efficient. 
  Notably, this finding is not a mere theoretical curiosity, as it 
  provides a concrete basis for a recent empirical observation regarding 
  the interplay between privacy budget and model accuracy. 
  Ultimately, this research contributes to the growing body of work 
  focused on the interplay between data characteristics, learning algorithms, 
  and the desired level of privacy, with implications for the design of 
  DP analysis methods.
